title: k=3 Birthday Problem: Extension Counting Framework
content: The **k=3 birthday problem** asks: how many people are needed for a 50% chance that 3+ share a birthday? (Answer: 88, vs 23 for k=2.) This file develops the **extension-counting framework**: adding one person to a valid $n$-assignment, the number of valid days is $d - \#\{\text{full days}\}$. This enables a recursion for the exact probability $P(\text{all assignments have} < 3 \text{ per day})$.
mathContext: An assignment $f: \text{Fin}(n) \to \text{Fin}(d)$ is **k-valid** if every day has $< k$ people: $|\text{fiber}(j)| < k$ for all $j$. For $k=3$: max 2 per day. The probability of no triple coincidence is $|\{f: \text{k-valid}\}|/d^n$. The **pigeonhole limit**: when $n \geq (k-1)d$, every valid assignment must have some day full by the fiber-sum constraint. For $k=3$, $d=365$: the threshold is $n=88$ for $P > 0.5$.
prerequisites: Fin n → Fin d as assignment type

title: fiberAt and Fiber Partition Sum
content: **fiberAt(f, j)**: the set of people assigned to day $j$ — `Finset.univ.filter (fun i => f i = j)`. **fiberAt_sum**: $\sum_j |\text{fiberAt}(f,j)| = n$ — people are partitioned by day. Proved via `Finset.card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise` from Mathlib, which unifies `Fintype.card_fin n = n` with the fiber decomposition.
mathContext: `Finset.card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise` states: for $f: s \to t$, $|s| = \sum_{j \in t} |f^{-1}(j) \cap s|$. Here $s = \text{Fin}(n)$ and $t = \text{Fin}(d)$, with $|\text{Fin}(n)| = n$ via `Fintype.card_fin`. The proof applies this with `simp only` to simplify the fiberwise formula, then `linarith` to close the numeric equality $n = n$. This fiber partition is the foundation for all subsequent counting arguments.

title: Full-Days Bound: Below Pigeonhole, Not All Days Full
content: **daysWithExactly(f, m)**: days with exactly $m$ people. **fullDays(f, k)**: days with $k-1$ people (at capacity). **fullDays_card_le**: $|\text{fullDays}| \leq d$ trivially. **fullDays_lt_d**: if $n < (k-1)d$, then $|\text{fullDays}| < d$. Proof by contradiction: if all $d$ days were full, $\sum_j |\text{fiber}(j)| = (k-1)d > n$, contradicting the fiber sum identity.
mathContext: The contradiction in `fullDays_lt_d`: assume $|\text{fullDays}| \geq d$. Since $|\text{fullDays}| \leq d$ always (it's a subset of $\text{Fin}(d)$), we get $|\text{fullDays}| = d$, so `fullDays f k = Finset.univ` via `Finset.eq_univ_of_card`. Then $\sum_j |\text{fiber}(j)| \geq \sum_j (k-1) = (k-1)d$ (since each day $j$ is full, so $|\text{fiber}(j)| \geq k-1$). But $\sum_j |\text{fiber}(j)| = n < (k-1)d$ by hypothesis — contradiction via `omega`.

title: extensionCount: Valid Days for New Person
content: **extensionCount(f, k)** = $d - |\text{fullDays}(f, k)|$ — the number of valid days for placing a new person. **extensionCount_le**: $\leq d$ trivially. **extensionCount_pos**: below pigeonhole limit, at least one valid day. **fullDays_k3**: for $k=3$, full days = doubled days (days with exactly 2 people). **extension_possible_k3**: for $n < 2d$ with valid $k=3$ assignment, extension is always possible.
mathContext: For $k=3$: a new person can go on any day with $< 2$ people — the `extensionCount` is $d - \#\{\text{doubled days}\}$. `extension_possible_k3` specializes `extensionCount_pos` to $k=3$: use $n < 2d$ and `hvalid : \forall j, |\text{fiber}(j)| \leq 2$. The proof is just `apply extensionCount_pos f 3 (by omega) (by omega) hvalid` — the omega calls verify $1 \leq 3$ and $n < (3-1) \cdot d = 2d$. The `extensionCount` is the key to the recursive formula for counting valid assignments.

title: Day Type Decomposition: 0/1/2 People Per Day
content: For a valid $k=3$ assignment: **day_type_trichotomy** — each day $j$ has 0, 1, or 2 people (by `omega` from the bound $\leq 2$). **day_types_disjoint_01/02/12** — the three sets are pairwise disjoint (by `Finset.disjoint_filter.mpr` + `omega`). **day_types_cover** — together they cover $\text{Fin}(d)$. **day_types_sum_d** — their cardinalities sum to $d$.
mathContext: `day_types_sum_d` chains: $(|E| + |S|) + |D| = |E \cup S| + |D|$ (by `card_union_of_disjoint` for E∪S and D) $= |(E \cup S) \cup D|$ (by `card_union_of_disjoint`) $= |\text{univ}| = d$ (using `day_types_cover`). The `Finset.card_union_of_disjoint` requires the disjointness theorems. The pairwise disjointness proofs all use `Finset.disjoint_filter.mpr` with `omega`: if $j$ has 0 people, it can't also have 1, etc.

title: Restriction: Removing Last Person Preserves Validity
content: **fiberAt_restrict_le**: the restricted assignment $f \circ \text{Fin.castSucc}$ (ignoring the last person) has weakly smaller fibers: $|\text{fiberAt}(f \circ \text{castSucc}, j)| \leq |\text{fiberAt}(f, j)|$. **restrict_valid**: if $f: \text{Fin}(n+1) \to \text{Fin}(d)$ is valid, so is its restriction to $\text{Fin}(n)$.
mathContext: `Fin.castSucc : Fin n → Fin (n+1)` embeds the first $n$ elements. `f ∘ Fin.castSucc` is the restriction of $f$ to the first $n$ people. The fiber of the restriction is a subset of the fiber of $f$ (the last person is in the fiber of $f$ but not of the restriction). `fiberAt_restrict_le` proves this via `Finset.card_le_card` and `Finset.mem_filter` — any element of the restricted fiber is also in the full fiber. `restrict_valid` composes with `fullDays_lt_d` to enable the recursive structure: going from $n+1$ back to $n$ gives a valid assignment.
